# Copper August 2010 

- Picking up from their rising trend from the end of July, copper prices firmed still further in early August by opening at $7334/t ($3.33/lb) on the 2nd.  The following week saw the continuation of this upward trend, with cash closing at $7423/t on the 9th, but new data sets out of China were taken poorly by the market, and swiftly brought an end to the 16-day price rally. Through to the 12th, copper prices fell back, prompted China but also by a strengthening of the US$ vs. the euro.  Then that US$-euro view was reversed over the space of that weekend, and by the following Monday 16th copper resumed its upward trend to $7442/t (cash - $3.38/lb) by the 19th, the highest price since April 27th ($7643/t - $3.47/lb).  However, that August 19th price was the high for the month, as daily declines through to the 25th had copper prices re-testing the $7000/t level ($3.18/lb - cash). 

- For the second consecutive month we have nudged our demand forecast for 2010 upwards, but this time it is China and Europe that have been showing the more favourable conditions.  For all of the ongoing macro-economic commentary, which has largely been bearish of late, there continues to be a noticeable disconnect between general economic data releases and demand for metals. 

- We have been surprised by just how much No.2 (and lower grades of) scrap has been available to the Chinese (and some other) markets thus far in 2010.  Originally, we had expected copper unit availability from scrap to be rather anaemic due to the lack of demolition and new construction work being carried out within the mature economies. However, recent analysis points to a “gap” in new refined copper production in China and elsewhere that can only have been met by higher scrap utilisation. 

- August has seen a pick up in activity in the spot copper concentrates market with a number of miners (predominantly Latin American) issuing tenders over the past month.  In total we estimate that there was in excess of 100kt of material transacted.  Interestingly, despite a lack of buying interest from the smelting sector, bidding on most of this tonnage was reportedly aggressive, with terms remaining at relatively low levels.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Copper prices push north again in August…** Picking up from their rising trend from the end of July, copper prices firmed still further in early August by easing past the $7121/t ($3.23/lb) average cash price of the final week of last month and opening at $7334/t ($3.33/lb) on August 2<sup>nd</sup> .  Despite the release of disappointing OECD leading indicators on August 6<sup>th</sup> and discouraging jobless claims data from the USA, copper ended this first week on a 3.5-month high at $7418/t (cash - $3.36/lb).  The start of the following week saw the resumption of this upward trend, with cash closing at $7423/t on the 9<sup>th</sup> , but new data sets out of China were taken poorly by the market, and swiftly brought an end to the 16day price rally across the entire metals complex. 

**Chinese government “closes” inefficient metals capacity** The price downturn was seemingly sparked by a new policy enactment by the Chinese Industry Ministry to close energy-inefficient metals factories by the end of September in order to meet tough year-end emissions targets.  While information was sparse, the market responded bearishly, believing that the measure would shrink refined metals output and, perhaps more importantly, semis processing activity even beyond what the macro-economic data sets were predicting for the second half of the year.  It took a couple of days, however, for interested parties to obtain the list of required plant closures and for a correct interpretation of what the measure would really mean for copper – which, for copper, turned out to be a non-event (see CONCENTRATES MARKETS).  Over the balance of the week, through to the 12<sup>th</sup> , copper prices fell back, prompted by this latest Chinese puzzle but also by a strengthening of the US$ _vs._ the euro, which once again focused attention on the apparently worsening condition of the US economy.  Despite a minor recovery on the Friday 13<sup>th</sup> , copper prices were still $200/t (cash) down on the week at almost $7200/t ($3.27/lb). 

**Higher H1 supply kept in check by equally strong revisions to demand** That US$-euro view reversed over the space of that weekend, and by the following Monday 16<sup>th</sup> copper resumed its upward trend once again to move up to $7442/t (cash - $3.38/lb) by the 19<sup>th</sup> , the highest price since April 27<sup>th</sup> ($7643/t - $3.47/lb).  Widespread discussion regarding global mine supply constraints and declining product stocks on exchanges were behind the price support, coupled with a firming belief that metal demand has been stronger than appreciated during the first half of the year. While our own reassessment of the fundamentals has increased supply during this period, the even stronger uptake in demand has kept the surplus to a level that in absolute tonnage terms could be considered a balanced market. However, that August 19<sup>th</sup> price h

igh now seems a distant memory, as daily declines through to the 25th had copper prices re-testing the $7000/t level ($3.18/lb - cash), with a raft of negative macro-economic data from Europe and the US combining with an upward trend in Shanghai metal stocks to overturn the flirt with newly-found, albeit cautious, optimism. #### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 9000

**SHFE stocks turn up** Unlike the trend of the past three months, copper metal stocks held on the Shanghai exchange were frequently reported in the industrial press as “moving up” during August. More accurately put, they did edge up by 9kt from the end of July to stand at 113.4kt by August 12th , but they have since dropped again to 110.6t on the 26th . That said, the market has become accustomed to seeing month-on-month stock declines on the SHFE, and so any deviance from that pattern was inevitably to be interpreted as bearish news. In a way, this relative “stability” in stocks will partly reflect the lower mid-summer end-user demand and the 6% higher imports of refined metal in July over June. This latter event was expected, given the favourable arbitrage between the LME and the SHFE over the prior two-month period. With that arbitrage window closing since early July, we anticipate that September’s refined metal imports level (and perhaps even this month’s) will fall away unless Chinese refined output sinks even further than it did in July. Ending July at the 413kt level, they reached a low of 401.3kt at the close on the 25th . The last time the Exchange had this level of copper stocks was early December 2009, and 28kt of cancelled warrants point to further imminent reductions. As per the the last few months, warehouses in New Orleans (down 5.75kt) and Busan in South Korea (6.275kt) saw the largest month-on-month withdrawals, followed by Mobile (-2.5kt) and Bilbao (-1.05kt), but these were partly offset by gains in St Louis (+2.75kt), Singapore (+1kt) and Johor in Malaysia (+1kt). #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 600 Refined Imports 400

**Spot premia weaken** With Chinese copper demand going through its seasonal lull, it is no surprise that spot markets and premia have weakened thus far into the month. Imported cathode premia on a spot basis fell from over US$140/t at the end of last month to US$100-120/t during the first half of August, with more recent numbers testing the US$60-80/t range. Premia in the US have remained flat at the 6.0-6.5c/lb level, although the trucking availability issue that we noted Metals Market Service Monthly Update - August 2010 Page 3 of 22 Copper Monthly Update last month which had pushed spot copper cathode premia up to as high as 7.0c/lb has reportedly eased. Meanwhile, European premia have held reasonably constant at $75-90/t. **Chinese processors now looking for scrap…** One of the reasons behind the weakening Chinese cathode premia is that interest in scrap among processors has increased as copper prices have made primary metal more expensive. July’s official copper scrap imports of 378kt were up by 7% on June’s, putting the year-on-year increase at 10%. But we also suspect that domestic scrap _availability_ should have been higher, given the myriad of scrapping schemes promoted by the government, even if the semis sector itself was not overly concerned about making use of it. **..while the primary sector has been using more of it throughout H1** While scrap use has not been a very important feature in the Chinese semis market until now, it has been of much more significance to overall copper cathode production by smelters and electro-refiners. We have been surprised by just how much No.2 (and lower grades of) scrap has been available to the Chinese (and some other) markets thus far in 2010. Originally, we had expected copper unit availability from scrap to be rather anaemic due to the lack of demolition and new construction work being carried out within the mature economies. However, recent analysis points to a “gap” in new refined copper production in China and elsewhere, namely Germany, Poland and Russia relative to what we know to have been the respective primary raw materials supplies. #### **Key changes in H1 2010 refined copper make up vs H1 2009*

Furthermore, with copper in concentrate stocks being at very low levels, the uplift in refined production cannot be accounted for by any significant draw down in concentrate stocks. We believe, then, that the only apparent way for this differential to be reconciled is by increased scrap use. The table above takes into account our various assumptions on traditional intermediates feedstock based on latest trade data and reported output, and shows that scrap use at smelters and refineries must have increased on a global basis by around 320kt H1 2010 _vs._ H1 2009, or by around 24%. This has been broken down on a country-by-country basis looking at refined production growth and considering the changes in make-up of refined output vis-а-vis concentrate availability, blister trade, and changes in SxEw output, with the implicit assumption that the balance had to have been met by scrap. Although there are some shortcomings with this analysis, such as the difficulty in country-by-country stock movements, we have worked on the basis that with copper prices being so high and credit availability still being somewhat restrained, best practice policies of minimising inventories would mean that stock movements should not have been significant. China leads the way in terms of the uplift in scrap use, despite the noted big increase in concentrate and blister imports in H1 2010 (see CONCENTRATES MARKETS), but a number of European smelter/refineries have also benefitted from an uplift in scrap availability, notably in Germany, Belgium, Poland and Austria. As with China, these countries have also promoted low-finance or subsidised scrapping schemes, and we have to assume that the bonus secondary metallics have been the result. **Firmer market balance in H2 brings hike in price forecast** Although our changes to refined production (up by 347kt) since last month and demand (+349kt) are finely matched, what has changed significantly is the market balance for the second half of this year. We are now anticipating almost 170kt less refined production in the second half than we were last month, and 70kt higher demand, leaving our H2 market balance in deficit by c.35kt rather than a surplus of

200kt. Consequently, our average price range for the period has firmed to $7070-7300/t ($3.21-3.31/lb) from $6500-6800/t. Additionally, our expected metal market deficit for 2011 has been pushed further out from 265kt to almost 350kt under stronger demand fundamentals, and we have therefore raised our forecast price for the year from just over $7000/t to almost $7500/t ($3.40/lb). For all of the ongoing macro-economic commentary, which has largely been bearish of late, there continues to be a noticeable disconnect between general economic data releases and demand for metals. While we still believe that during the first half of the year metals demand was principally led by re-stocking efforts across geographic markets, China and some leading consumer areas of Europe have also witnessed a fair share of underlying demand growth. Although the latter once again appears to be fading away across Europe and the USA, Chinese markets continue to benefit from consumer demand growth as well as replacement requirements (i.e. repairs), following such natural disasters as the recent flooding from Typhoon Conson across the southern provinces of Yunnan, Sichuan, Hunan, Jiangxi and Anhui. To the east, temperatures are averaging 3-5 degrees hotter than usual, and stocks of some copper-intensive consumer goods, such as air conditioners, while they have been high, have dwindled (see belo

w).  With European demand also being edged up by c.110kt, thanks largely to the resilient German automotive market, our global copper demand forecast for 2010 now stands at 18.675Mt, or 8.6% up on last year. 

### **USA** 

**US Fed shows some signs of nervousness over the economy** The Federal Reserve this month acknowledged a weakening economic outlook by opting to re-invest the US$160Bn in proceeds received from holdings purchased via “quantitative easing” in 2009 that had reached maturity instead of using them to shrink the deficit.   This suggests that interest and borrowing rates will be kept low in order to promote corporate lending, but is also likely to mean that monetary tightening will be delayed until the second half of next year.   Select recent macro economic data continue to show the balancing act that the country is going through.  Industrial production grew at an unexpectedly high 1.1% last month, taking overall IP growth since the low of June 2009 to 9.2%.  However, to put this into some perspective, IP still needs to grow by a further 7.6% to get back to pre-crisis levels. 

**Manufacturing coming into line with demand** The main debate for metals demand this year has been the re-stocking cycle and if/when underlying demand would take over.  What we have seen in copper and other metals is that producers and consumers at all links along the chain have been as cautious in re-stocking as they have been in matching new fabrication rates to orders.  In the US, at least, we believe that the re-stocking phase is coming to an end, and that new manufacturing rates are now matching demand much more closely.  Effectively, this means a continuation of the “handto-mouth” existence, with all elements in the supply-demand chain keeping stock to a minimum, even at the risk of not being able to satisfy spot market requirements as they arise.  This is not so encouraging for near-term metals demand because other macro-economic indicators, such as retail sales and employment figures, are weak, and this is likely to cap consumption.  The consumer confidence index in July, for example, hit a five-month low. 

**Construction sector data less than inspiring** With construction accounting for 50% of US copper demand, it is difficult to remain optimistic when most indices for the sector continue to fall.  Despite the lowest mortgage rates in years and relatively low buying prices, sales of existing homes in the US (which account for 90% of total home sales) fell in July by over 27% to a seasonally-adjusted annual rate of 3.83M units.  This was the lowest rate in 15 years, according to the National Association of Realtors, and the largest month-on-month fall since 1968.  Furthermore, the decline was noted across all geographic regions but particularly apparent in the low- to mid-price range which had benefitted the most from the now-expired government tax breaks up to April this year.  Meanwhile, sales of new homes (the “top-up” 10% of total sales) fell

by 12.4% in July from June to an annualised rate of 226k units, and this was the slowest rate since records began in 1963. The inventory of unsold homes now extends over 12 months at current sales rates, which is the highest in ten years and more than double the level that is usually accepted as being sufficient to support prices and ongoing sales. Tightening lending standards have offset the potential improvement in home sales that would normally be seen with mortgage interest rates that are frequently under 5%. The threat of unemployment is also hindering mortgage applications. Meanwhile, the home builder index fell again by a point in August to 13, which indicates that any improvement in the construction sector for the next six months is remote. **Auto sales strong in July…** Other sectors that are important to copper demand in the US, though, remain strong. Total vehicle assemblies, on a seasonally-adjusted basis, rose to an annualised rate of 8.53M units, which is the highest rate in two years. The gains came almost entirely from the light trucks market, with car production relatively unchanged. Inventories decreased by three days to 52 days, indicating that producers continue to show restraint. Automotive sales were also strong in July, up by 5.2% year on year to 1.05M units ( _vs._ 984k units in June), but fleet sales rose by a much stronger rate (up 40% year on year) than retail (down by 3.8% year on year), and this is masking the underlying weakness in consumer demand. **Brass mill production edges lower** Following the path of its sister products in wire rod, US brass mill products output has trended lower over the last few months. Copper and copper alloy semis output of 409kt (metric) for January to May this year was up by 13% on the same period last year, although that did cover the trough in the cycle. Although pure Metals Market Service Monthly Update - August 2010 Page 6 of 22 Copper Monthly Update copper semis production tailed off slightly (from 203kt to 194kt), output of _alloy_ semis surged from 163kt to 222kt. However, as with wire rod data, we note that the recent high was in March; with the house buying incentives falling away in April-May, we doubt that these markets will pick up before this year is out. #### **US brass mill shipments – (kt)** 30 95

### **China** **Leading indicators supportive of slowdown policy** July data for China continue to support our view that the country is adequately managing its soft landing for the second half of this year. Fixed asset investment eased further to 24.9% year to date in July, from 25.5% in June, as growth in property investment slowed to 33% year on year in July from over 38% in June

.  Meanwhile, industrial production increased by 13.4%, down slightly from June’s 13.7%.  July’s export growth, while strong at 38%, is expected to ease in August, due partly to weakening external demand but also to an end to export tax rebates on some lower-value products this month.  The headline PMI index, as well as both the new orders and output components, fell below the 50 level in July, reinforcing the belief that growth will continue to slow in the coming months. 

**Q3 weak period for Chinese copper…** This relative declining macro-economic picture will be matched by equally declining metals-related data over the course of this quarter, which is traditionally the weakest time of the year for metals demand in China.  Wire rod production into August is thought to be at the lowest level seen thus far this year, but with some plants closed for summer holidays, this can be expected and should reverse in September.  Order books for copper semis for general consumer goods are reportedly sustaining the low level seen in July thus far into August. Some middle- to low-end copper alloy semis manufacturers have seen their orders fall this month by about 20% from the recent peaks of May to June.  Declining auto production and sales in July and August, and production of units such as air conditioners, there will be a seasonally-driven dip. 

**..but market conditions should soon change…** Most of the products from these middle- to low-end semis makers end up in home electrical goods and appliances, and markets for these are suffering from low export demand and high domestic inventories, but this latter situation could soon be about to change.  Q4 is usually the high point for copper demand, and so these semis producers are naturally expecting an improvement in orders, which would mop up some excess product stock.  But recent power brownouts and government-driven electricity cutbacks to high power-consuming sectors in Zhejiang and Jiangsu provinces will limit forward-looking semis output from these regions.  With Zhejiang accounting for 30% of the nation’s copper consumption, this should firstly draw down product inventories as consumers scramble to cover for the anticipated Q4 demand.  If the brownouts continue into October – or even until the end of the year, as some source say, then copper semi manufacturing will pick up at idle capacity elsewhere.  Therefore, we do not believe that this government-led initiative to improve energy efficiency by 20% by the end of the year will stifle copper processing, but merely re-locate it. 

**..giving a strong performance this year** Ultimately, though, the weak third quarter in China will be more than offset by market strength during the rest of the year.  Already we have seen a need to increase our H1 demand estimates from last month’s 3.551Mt to a shade over 3.6Mt, and our revised H2 forecast demand of 3.762Mt will mean that China’s year on year copper demand forecast growth now approaches 13%, rather than t

he 10% we had previously considered. And Metals Market Service Monthly Update - August 2010 Page 7 of 22 Copper Monthly Update the longer-term forecast still looks strong: only this month, the State Grid (SGCC), China’s major power grid operator, announced plans to build a network of ultra high-voltage (UHV) power transmission lines by 2020. During this current 12th 5-year plan, SGCC will complete the construction of UHV lines in northern, eastern and central China with lines as high as 1000 KV, which is double the existing network capacity. To date, most UHV cables have been imported from Japan and Europe, but SGCC will endeavour to produce the cable in China, driving the demand for copper rod for many years. #### **Chinese production of copper semis – (kt)** 80 1000

**Plans for new semis plants continue to come forward** The announcement from the SGCC was followed up (separately) by a statement from Jiangxi Copper Corp – already the nation’s largest refined copper producer and processor – that it intends to establish a new base for copper processing in the southern province of Guangzhou, in Zhencheng City. At 400kt/a, it would almost double the company’s existing capacity of copper semis, and comes with an investment tag of 2Bn yuan. Last year, JCC says it produced 484kt of copper products from 450kt of theoretical annual capacity installed, and its year-end 2009 target for 2010 was the same; clearly, its latest downstream investment plan is sorely required. Other company investments during the month were announced by Huigang Copper, which wants to set up a 750m yuan, 100kt/a capacity copper rod and bar facility in the Suixi economic development zone, Huaibei City, Anhui province; and by Chunlei Copper Semis Co, which has begun construction of its proposed 50kt/a capacity copper sheet and plate facility in Shanxi province. Meanwhile, Jiangnan Metal Products Co commissioned its 180m yuan, 30kt/a copper tube and rod plant in Xingan Country, Jiangxi on August 5th. ### **Europe** **European copper demand increased to 2.9Mt** We have increased our forecast for European copper demand this year from 2.796Mt to 2.906Mt, given the stronger first four to five months of the year than previously anticipated, especially in the industrial powerhouses of Germany and Italy. That said, weakening economic data into July suggest that the second half will result in slightly lower copper demand, and our H1 _vs._ H2 demand profile of 1.472Mt _vs._ 1.434Mt reflects this. European industrial production fell month on month in June on a seasonally adjusted basis, led by a decline in production of consumer durables. The acceleration in growth rates seen earlier in Q2 and before h

as been largely reliant upon government policy and the inventory re-stocking cycle, and moving forward we are probably heading for a higher weighting of austerity measures which will restrain growth well into 2011. Early August indicators show lower performances than in July, but this might still be a reflection of summer shut-downs rather than the start of the more widespread downturn in business levels. **Germany leads the europack** The EU manufacturing PMI’s rebounded in July, with Germany leading the way. Here, auto production in particular has continued to recover, despite July’s seasonal drop in auto output of 418kt units (down by 2.9% year on year). While there is widespread expectation that the second half of this year will see some level of decline from Q2 levels, for the present time we are not seeing any dramatic reversal of these gains. Aurubis, Europe’s largest copper producer, has benefitted from the stronger auto and energy sectors, and posted its fifth straight quarterly improvement in aggregate wire rod and shapes production. At 260kt for the March-June quarter (Q3 for Aurubis’ reporting), this exceeded the 246kt produced in the final quarter ahead of the economic crisis (calendar Q3 2008). In other products, Aurubis has continued to increase output of pre-rolled strip (56kt in Q2 vs. 50kt in Q1 2010 – matching Q2 2008’s 58kt level), while strip and wire from the former Prymetall subsidiary held steady at 13.1kt. **Romania’s wire rod sector draws on imports** Earlier this year we noted that Romania’s sole copper wire rod facility was rumoured to have been closed down during the final quarter of 2009, presumably a victim of the global recession. Even though we have yet to receive official confirmation of this, the fact that both domestic production and imports of cathode have been zero this year would indicate that the Cuprom wire rod plant at Zalau has gone the same way as its sister smelter-refinery complex at Baie Mare and closed. Instead, Cuprom has turned to imports of rod to keep its wiremaking equipment gainfully employed. **Polish wire rod production increased** First half refined cathode production figures from KGHM, plus trade data to May, have prompted us to increase Poland’s rod production forecast for this year. Higher cathode production and net imports should enable KGHM to produce c.205kt of wire rods this year at its Cedynia facility, _vs._ our former forecast of 156kt and 2009’s actual output of 191kt. Judging by the company’s H1 cathode performance, though, H2 rod output will tail off slightly as 268kt (52%) of the full year’s cathode target of 512kt has already been produced. Clearly rod sales are proving to be more resilient than we had anticipated, largely due to the improving construction sector, and this has encouraged us to raise forecast 2011 rod output as well, from our former 165kt to 212kt. This keeps in-house conversion of cathode to wire rod at c.40%, which is in line with recent years, albeit slightly lower than the 48% seen earlier this decade. KGHM is continuing to improve the capacity

utilisation rate from its value-added product range via the UPCAST oxygen-free rod line investment, which it completed in September 2007. Last year, 13.8kt came off this 15kt/a capacity line, up from 11.8kt the prior year. ### **Japan** **Japan’s low June IP creating concern…** As we noted last month, recent data releases from Japan have been bearing down on the country’s ability to show economic resilience in the face of the economic crisis, and this month’s batch has done nothing to reverse that concern. Although up by 17% year on year, June’s industrial production rate fell by 1.5% on May’s, mainly due to lower auto output and electronic devices, as stimulus measures have faded away. This contraction comes in spite of the fact that Japan continues to re-build inventories, which has been the case for much of this year. With the recent political instability and talk of austerity measures, and a central bank that appears unwilling to act further, the possibility of domestic demand improving soon are slim. Gains from exports are being hampered by the strengthening yen as well as economic uncertainty in Japan’s main exports markets of the US and Europe, and this is reflected in the country’s PMI’s, which declined in July for both orders and output, and point to further near-term slowdowns. Consequently, the stronger than expected re-stocking phase has lifted our H1 copper demand from our previous assessment of 428kt to a revised 511kt, and pushed up our full-year tally to 990kt from last month’s 950kt. But the expectations of a poorer second half will see demand pull back to c.480kt. **..but copper data remain strong** In the meantime, though, copper industry-related data continue to show how strong the first half has been. Brass mill output for June, at 76.4kt, continued the upward trend that has been in place since December last year, and was the highest monthly total since September 2008. The Japan Copper and Brass Manufacturers’ Association reported that steady demand from the semi-conductor and automobiles sectors, plus higher exports to China and South East Asia, were the mainstays behind the growth. However, the JCBMA noted that the construction sector remains a drag on continued market improvements, and despite housing construction picking up moderately in July from a very weak June, no one is under any illusions about the depression that the sector is in. Average build volumes are 30% down this year from the past decade average, and 45% down on the 1990’s average, and high unemployment levels and low job security will keep the lid on new mortgage applications for the foreseeable future. **Chinese copper concentrate imports contract for the third successive month** As mentioned, after a strong start to the year China’s appetite for foreign copper concentrates has waned in recent months.  July’s imports, which totalled 466.5kdmt, were down by 7.6% relative to the same period in 2009 making this the third successive month of year-onyear declines (May and June were lower by 6% and 16% respectively).  Part of the reason for the reduction in imports relates to several smelters being shut for maintenance during July, including

Chifeng Jinjian (120kt/a) in Inner Mongolia, Dongying (100kt/a) in Liaoning province and Jinlong (400kt/a) in Anhui province, which shut for three weeks in August. Also, with Yunnan Copper’s 210kt/a smelter out of action for an extended period (July 2010 through to perhaps April next year) for a major re-build, this will cut the company’s requirement for imported concentrate feed.  Typically, Yunnan buys 750kt/a of concentrates with 500kt/a allocated to Yunnan province for its main smelter and other smaller plants in the region plus a further 250kt/a for its Jinfeng smelter in Inner Mongolia.  As a consequence of the shutdown of the main smelter Yunnan’s purchases are expected to fall to around 600kt in 2010.  Given the remote location of its main smelter in relation to eastern seaboard ports, the economics of importing spot concentrates in the context of low TC/RCs and high inland freight costs (~$30-$40/t) make this business particularly unfavourable at the present time.  However, Yunnan will be able to maintain normal refined production rates by importing large amounts of blister from its part-owned Chambishi smelter in Zambia.  According to trade statistics, imports from this African country increased to 81kt during the first seven months of this year compared with only 23kt over the same period last year.  Later in 2010 some shipments of Chambishi blister will be switched to Yunnan’s 100kt/a joint venture refinery in Qingyuan (Guangdong province) which is expected to be commissioned in October.  It remains unclear whether the Yunnan smelter shutdown is related more to a maintenance requirement or to current market conditions.  Ultimately, spot terms will have to rise if China continues to refrain from purchasing material because the only other market that is active at these low terms is India and the demand outlook for spot concentrates there appears to be rather moderate over the balance of the year.

**Kolwezi Tailings debacle continues** There have been further developments in the ongoing dispute over the ownership of the Kolwezi Tailings project in the DRC.  On August 20<sup>th</sup> ENRC announced that a wholly owned subsidiary had privately purchased a 50.5% stake in Camrose Resources which holds indirect interests in five copper-cobalt exploitation licences including a 70% interest in the Kolwezi Tailings site through Metalkol SARL, a subsidiary of Camrose’s Highwind Group.  ENRC has stated that development of the Kolwezi Tailings project is subject to feasibility studies being completed and that Metalkol has not acquired any infrastructure or equipment at the site.  Meanwhile, First Quantum has reported that on August 19<sup>th</sup> the tribunal at the International Chamber of Commerce in Paris had issued two procedural orders.  The first prohibits the DRC and Gecamines from taking any action to transfer or allow the transfer of the Kolwezi Tailings exploitation permit covering the Kolwezi Project.  The second order prohibits the DRC and Gecamines from taking any action to enforce a March 10, 2010 judgment of the Appeal Court of Kinshasa that required a subsidiary of First Quantum and Kingamyambo Musonoi Tailings SARL, the Congolese company which was developing the Kolwezi project, to pay damages totalling more than US$12Bn to Gecamines, the Mining Registry and the DRC. The tribunal’s orders are to remain in place until such time as the tribunal has made a decision on the First Quantum’s request for interim measures. 

**ENRC to expand Chambishi** ENRC is looking to expand the capacity of its recently-acquired Chambishi copper-cobalt plant in Zambia from 25kt/a Cu to 55kt/a Cu by 2013.  The company will also improve the quality of the copper cathode through installing an Sx circuit at the plant.  Current practice is to produce electrowon cathode from leach solutions without this processing stage which affects cathode quality.  ENRC acquired the Chambishi plant in February 2010 and produced 660t of Cu and 965t of Co in Q2.  The company also owns the Luita SxEw complex in DRC which produced 4.5kt Cu in the second quarter. 

**Mirador project gets green light** Ecuacorriente, which is owned by China’s CRCC-Tongguan joint venture, expects construction activity to commence at its Mirador copper project in Ecuador in November.  The initial investment is put at $631M, although an additional $100M will be required to build an HEP plant for the project.  The company aims to be in production by Q4 2012 with a phase I output rate of 60kt/a of copper-in-concentrates.  Ecuacorriente’s Panantza San Carlos project, also in Ecuador, is at an advanced exploration stage and the joint venture hopes to establish a 285kt/a copper operation by Q1 2015 at an estimated capital cost of $1.3Bn.  In April 2008 mine project activity in Ecuador was halted as th

e Government sought to formulate a new legal framework in order to increase the country’s income from mining. A new mining law was approved in January 2010 that includes a minimum 5% royalty tax and a 70% windfall profits tax. Ecuacorriente hopes to receive a new environmental permit for the exploitation stage of Panantza; the company currently has an exploration permit for the project. **Gold Hawk looks to acquire former US copper mine** Canada’s Gold Hawk Resources has signed a letter of intent to acquire the Oracle Ridge copper mine in Arizona. This is a small-scale underground operation that was opened in 1991 and produced 3-5kt/a of copper-in-concentrates through to 1996 when it was shut down due to low copper prices. Proven and probable reserves are put at 7.4Mt grading 2.33% Cu at a 1.5% Cu cut-off grade. **Russian Copper Co. to modernise its Karabash smelter** Russian Copper Co. aims to modernise and expand its Karabash smelter in the Urals to raise capacity from 90kt/a to 120kt/a at a projected cost of $310M. The smelter’s output was estimated to be 60kt in last year and 34kt in H1 2010. Feed for the plant is sourced from RCC’s Aleksandrinskoe and Barsuchy Log mines in Russia and from the Koktaus mine in Kazakhstan. Prior to the global financial crisis the company had sought to raise overall copper output to 190kt/a but these plans were subsequently put on hold. **Equinox investigating major expansion at Lumwana** Equinox Minerals is considering an expansion at its Lumwana mine in Zambia. The current capacity of the mill is 20Mt/a and Equinox has awarded an engineering contract to Ausenco who is expected to announce the results of its work by Q1 2011. The company is targeting a throughput rate of 24Mt/a through de-bottlenecking the plant and a second stage expansion to 35Mt/a. Preliminary estimates suggest a three- to four-year timetable and a capital cost of $300 to $400M. Equinox produced 74.3kt of copper-in-concentrates in H1 2010 and expects this year’s overall output to be 135kt.
